exercises.prompt: On AWS, the first four addresses and the last address of every subnet are reserved. How many addresses can be assigned to machines in a subnet with the prefix `/26`?

feedback.message: Not yet — 64 is the size of a /26 block. Subtract the reserved addresses.
Close — 62 is the classic count for an on-premises subnet (network and broadcast addresses only). This provider reserves five.
Not yet — 251 is for a /24. A /26 is a quarter of that size.

exercises.solution: A `/26` fixes 26 of the 32 bits, leaving 6 bits: $2^6 = 64$ addresses. Five are reserved (the network address, three for the provider's router, DNS and future use, and the last address), leaving $64 - 5 = 59$. Other providers reserve four or five addresses per subnet; the lesson's advice stands everywhere — make subnets comfortably larger than you think you need.

exercises.prompt: A web server's subnet has a **stateless** network ACL whose only rules are: inbound, allow TCP to port 443 from `0.0.0.0/0`; outbound, allow TCP to port 443 to `0.0.0.0/0`; everything else denied. The server's **stateful** security group allows inbound TCP 443 from anywhere. The server is running, yet every browser's attempt to connect times out. Why?

options.label: The ACL drops the server's replies: they go to the browsers' ephemeral ports (typically 1024–65535), not to port 443
options.feedback: Yes. A stateless filter judges each packet alone, so the replies need their own outbound rule for the clients' ephemeral ports.

options.label: The security group drops the replies, because it has no outbound rule
options.feedback: Not yet — security groups are stateful: replies to an allowed inbound connection are allowed automatically.

options.label: Port 443 needs UDP as well as TCP
options.feedback: Not yet — HTTPS over TCP needs only TCP (HTTP/3 uses UDP, but browsers fall back to TCP). The problem is the direction and port of the replies.

options.label: The internet gateway blocks port 443 by default
options.feedback: Not yet — the gateway routes; filtering is done by the ACL and the security group.

hints: A reply packet from the server goes *from* port 443 *to* which port on the browser's machine?
Which of the two filters remembers connections, and which does not?
exercises.solution: When a browser connects, its packets go to the server's port 443 *from* an ephemeral port such as 51514 chosen by the browser's operating system. The server's replies go *from* 443 *to* 51514. The stateful security group recognises the replies as part of an allowed connection. The stateless ACL does not remember anything: its only outbound rule allows packets *to* port 443, so it drops replies to port 51514 — starting with the server's SYN-ACK, the second packet of the TCP handshake, which is why connections never open and time out. The fix is an outbound ACL rule allowing TCP to ports 1024–65535 (or simply relying on stateful security groups and leaving the ACL permissive).

exercises.prompt: An image-resizing service in São Paulo runs on 12 servers. Most requests take 20 ms, but large images take up to 2 s. Each server keeps a small in-memory cache of recently resized images, and some images are far more popular than others. Which load-balancing policy best combines short queues with useful caches?

options.label: Round robin
options.feedback: Not yet — round robin ignores how long requests take, so a server stuck on a 2-second image keeps receiving its share, and every server caches every image.

options.label: Least connections
options.feedback: Good for queues, but it scatters each image's requests over all 12 servers, so each cache holds a twelfth of the benefit.

options.label: Consistent hashing on the image's name
options.feedback: Great caches, but the server owning the most popular images may be overloaded, and its queue — and the tail latency — grows without bound.

options.label: Consistent hashing with bounded loads, on the image's name
options.feedback: Yes. Each image usually goes to the same server (warm cache), but a server already well above the average is skipped, so hot images cannot overload it.

hints: Two goals pull against each other: affinity (same image, same server) and balance.
Which policy in the lesson's simulation kept a short tail *and* fewer distinct keys per server?
exercises.solution: Caching wants **affinity** — each image to go to the same server — which consistent hashing gives. Variable request costs and skewed popularity want **load awareness**, or a hot image's server is overwhelmed, as the plain consistent-hashing row of the simulation showed (p99 of 14.8 s). **Consistent hashing with bounded loads** follows the ring but skips servers more than a fixed factor above the average, keeping most of the affinity (936 distinct keys per server instead of about 1500 in the simulation) and a tail close to least connections.

exercises.prompt: A submarine cable route from Lagos to a data centre in Lisbon is about 5,000 km long. Light in fibre travels about 200 km per millisecond. What is the smallest possible **round-trip** time over this route, in milliseconds, ignoring all equipment delays?

feedback.message: Close — 25 ms is one way. A round trip goes there and back.

hints: One way: distance divided by speed.
exercises.solution: One way takes $5000 / 200 = 25$ ms, so a round trip takes at least $50$ ms. Routers, retransmissions and queueing only add to this. A request that needs three round trips (TCP, TLS 1.3 and the request itself) on a new connection therefore waits at least 150 ms before the first byte of the answer, however fast the servers and links are.

exercises.prompt: A ticketing site in Seoul plans to move its traffic to a new region on Saturday by changing its DNS record to a new address. The record's TTL is currently 86,400 seconds (one day). What should the team do?

options.label: Lower the TTL (say to 60 s) at least a day before the move, change the address on Saturday, and raise the TTL again once the new region is stable
options.feedback: Yes. Resolvers that cached the old record with a one-day TTL may keep it for a day; lowering it first lets those copies expire before the change.

options.label: Change the address on Saturday; DNS changes reach everyone within seconds
options.feedback: Not yet — resolvers cache answers for the TTL. With a one-day TTL, some users would reach the old address until Sunday.

options.label: Set the TTL to 0 permanently, so that every lookup is fresh
options.feedback: Not yet — some resolvers ignore very low TTLs, and a permanent TTL of 0 multiplies DNS queries and adds a lookup to every connection. Low TTLs are for changes; raise them afterwards.

options.label: Turn off the old region at the moment of the change, so that clients are forced to look the name up again
options.feedback: Not yet — clients with a cached answer will simply fail to connect until their cache expires; they do not look the name up again just because the address stopped answering.

hints: How long may a resolver keep the old answer after you change it?
exercises.solution: A resolver that looked the name up just before the change may keep the old answer for the full TTL — here a day. So lower the TTL well in advance (at least one old TTL before the move), make the change, keep the old region serving until traffic to it has drained, and then raise the TTL again to reduce query load. Health-checked failover records or an anycast front end avoid the problem for unplanned failovers.

exercises.prompt: A video platform's CDN receives 50,000 requests per second for segments of its videos, with a hit ratio of 92%. A redesign of the cache keys raises the hit ratio to 98%. By how many requests per second does the load on the origin **fall**?

feedback.message: Not yet — 4,000 req/s is the origin load before the change. The question asks how much it falls.
Not yet — 1,000 req/s is the origin load after the change. Subtract it from the load before.

hints: Origin load = total requests × (1 − hit ratio).
Compute it at 92% and at 98%, then subtract.
exercises.solution: Before: $50{,}000 \times (1 - 0.92) = 4{,}000$ requests per second reach the origin. After: $50{,}000 \times (1 - 0.98) = 1{,}000$. The load falls by $3{,}000$ requests per second — a fourfold cut from a six-point change in hit ratio, because the origin sees the misses, not the hits.

exercises.prompt:
Write `sg_allows(rules, protocol, port, source)`, the inbound check of a stateful security group (replies are not your concern here). Each rule is a dict such as `{"protocol": "tcp", "ports": (443, 443), "source": "0.0.0.0/0"}`: `protocol` is `"tcp"`, `"udp"` or `"all"` (which matches any protocol and any port), `ports` is an inclusive range, and `source` is an IPv4 or IPv6 CIDR block. Return `True` if the packet — its protocol, destination port and source address (a string) — matches **at least one** rule; otherwise `False` (default deny). Use the standard `ipaddress` module.

The starter checks only the port.
exercises.starter:
import ipaddress

def sg_allows(rules, protocol, port, source):
    """Inbound check for a security group. rules is a list of dicts like
    {"protocol": "tcp", "ports": (443, 443), "source": "0.0.0.0/0"}; protocol may be
    "tcp", "udp" or "all" ("all" matches any protocol and port). Return True if the packet
    (protocol, destination port, source address) matches at least one rule."""
    for rule in rules:
        lo, hi = rule["ports"]
        if lo <= port <= hi:          # checks only the port...
            return True
    return False
exercises.tests:
web = [
    {"protocol": "tcp", "ports": (443, 443), "source": "0.0.0.0/0"},        # HTTPS from anywhere (IPv4)
    {"protocol": "tcp", "ports": (443, 443), "source": "::/0"},             # ... and IPv6
    {"protocol": "tcp", "ports": (22, 22), "source": "203.0.113.0/24"},     # SSH from the office only
    {"protocol": "tcp", "ports": (8000, 8100), "source": "10.20.0.0/16"},   # internal health checks
    {"protocol": "all", "ports": (0, 65535), "source": "10.20.5.17/32"},    # the monitoring host
]
assert sg_allows(web, "tcp", 443, "198.51.100.7")
assert sg_allows(web, "tcp", 443, "2001:db8::42")
assert sg_allows(web, "tcp", 22, "203.0.113.200")
assert not sg_allows(web, "tcp", 22, "198.51.100.7"), "SSH is open only to 203.0.113.0/24"
assert not sg_allows(web, "udp", 443, "198.51.100.7"), "the HTTPS rules are for TCP only"
assert sg_allows(web, "tcp", 8050, "10.20.9.9")
assert not sg_allows(web, "tcp", 8101, "10.20.9.9"), "8101 is outside the range 8000-8100"
assert not sg_allows(web, "tcp", 8050, "10.21.0.1"), "10.21.0.1 is not in 10.20.0.0/16"
assert sg_allows(web, "udp", 161, "10.20.5.17"), "an 'all' rule matches any protocol and port"
assert not sg_allows(web, "udp", 161, "10.20.5.18")
assert not sg_allows([], "tcp", 443, "198.51.100.7"), "no rules: everything is denied"
hints: A rule matches only if all three parts match: protocol, port range and source block.
`ipaddress.ip_address(source) in ipaddress.ip_network(cidr)` tests membership; an IPv6 address is simply never in an IPv4 network.
An `"all"` rule ignores the protocol and the port, but still checks the source.
